newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: FEATURE - Nicaraguans head to Costa Rica for jobs.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Nicaraguans head to Costa Rica for jobs.

text.p: Every morning they line the banks of Nicaragua's steamy San Juan River waiting to board flimsy boats to take them, legally or illegally, to neighbouring Costa Rica and better economic prospects.

Driven by poverty, more than 100 undocumented Nicaraguans a day pass through the tropical town of San Carlos near the Costa Rican border on their way to their wealthier neighbour, Lt. Anibal Sovalvarro, Nicaragua's immigration chief in San Carlos, told Reuters. From San Carlos, boats ferry illegal immigrants to one of eight unguarded crossing points on the border, where Costa Rican "coyotes" wait with trucks to take them to the farms and factories where they will work, Sovalvarro said.
"The flow is constant. There are so many 'blind spots' where there is no control that the Nicaraguans can enter without any trouble," he said.

Costa Rican authorities say about 500,000 undocumented Nicaraguans live in Costa Rica and they deport between 600 and 1,000 a week. Nicaragua's population is 4.3 million and it shares a sparsely populated 200-mile (320 km) jungle border with Costa Rica. It is the second poorest country in Latin America, with 50 percent unemployment.

Similar to the situation of undocumented Mexicans in the United States -- albeit on a much smaller scale -- the plight of undocumented Nicaraguans in Costa Rica has become a flashpoint in relations between the economically disparate neighbours.

"In Costa Rica I walk in fear that we will be picked up. Costa Ricans see us as garbage, that we're worthless old rags. But we're humans as well," said Gabriel Lopez, an undocumented Nicaraguan who had just been deported.

Reports of abuse of Nicaraguans by Costa Rican border guards or police regularly provoke diplomatic notes from the Nicaraguan government and complaints by human rights groups. When reports of mass deportations of Nicaraguans from Costa Rica circulated in the local media last week, Nicaraguan President Arnoldo Aleman weighed in, calling on Costa Ricans to treat the Nicaraguans with respect.

"If the mass deportations continue we will have to contact Costa Rican authorities the same way we did with the United States to request some more time, but above all to ask that they be treated with respect and consideration," he told reporters.

Costa Rican authorities said they do not discriminate against Nicaraguans, they just apply their immigration laws. "We are not carrying out a campaign against Nicaraguans, we have only been trying to deal with a situation that unfortunately is at very serious levels," Public Security Minister Laura Chinchilla said.

Walking through the Costa Rican jungle at a tiny crossing point called Papaturro, 21-year-old Sonia Garcia said that as a domestic servant in Costa Rica she will earn three times what she made in Nicaragua. "There is no work in Nicaragua and what there is pays nothing. I have three children and couldn't support them. Maybe I'll be able to send them something from here," she said.
She said she, like many undocumented Nicaraguans, planned to head home once she had saved up some money.

Most Nicaraguans in Costa Rica work harvesting crops, as domestic servants or in construction, Sovalvarro said. He said Costa Rica made it easy for Nicaraguans to cross the border illegally because it depended on cheap Nicaraguan labour, then deported the workers when they were no longer needed.
